author: buchanan_robert
text:
O’er the wide earth all night,
 A little brooklet played;

 The flowers about it slept,
 But when I woke, he started;
 And as the dawning light
 Woke him to wake me too,
 The music was his prayer:
 "Come and awake with me!"

author: cushag
text:
In the "House o' Luck"

At the House o' Muck, we know how to live —
For the house is ours an' all its crew;
We were born in it, an' we will die there wi',
An' no other place wud be so true.

The little girl dreamed of seeing the fluffy cat lying next to her on her small lap, purring softly to reassure itself before falling asleep quietly.

author: buchanan_robert
text:
In the darkness of the night,
A soft breeze brought a sigh,
As I lay awake, alone in my room,
With tears rolling down from my eyes.
In that moment, I felt so much pain,
Like an arrow piercing through my heart.
It's hard to forget the past,
But I know we must let go, or else we will be trapped.

author: cushag
text:
The River

By The Sea

I know a river that's blue,
But it ain't no fool,
It knows what 'appened to you,

And it never complains;
For it's the only one
That ever carried me for free--
With nothin' more than a pail,
An old man in the sun,

A big white horse and a load
Of sand from out in the sand:
They used to make up my soul,

author: emily_dickinson
text:
How shall I face my life, and what it is
 That makes me love this world so well?
 Shall I look back to yesterday's bliss,
 Or shall I turn and say farewell?

Hawaiian Volcanoes
By: William Wordsworth

The Hawaiian volcanoes are so wonderful,
With their bright green pastures and dark lava.
They have an endless supply of power,
But it is best to keep them at bay.

When they explode with force, it is quite dangerous,
To try to go near when you’re not prepared.
It can take many lives away,
And that is something I cannot bear.

I know not how to mourn thee;
Thy memory is an agony!

For all my heart would have given—
I could not love another as well !

Ilocano poet and activist, Salvador B. Olarte (1879-1960) has authored “Ami ti Nagbalinagan”, which is one of his earliest known poems to be published on a local paper.

It was written during Spanish colonial rule as part of the 15th anniversary celebration of an Ilocos newspaper. The text is taken from Olartea’s collection entitled Tagikulisang Tagipusuon: Mga Ubing Naibingkas na Tinulat ni Salvador B., where it was first published.

and to the desert land he fled;
his skin grew thin from hunger's sting,
while Philip sought out finer deeds.

from battle and death too close;
but life went on for him as best it could -
it always is when there's no choice.

to steal is wrong, although it seems so easy!

I am no longer your own,

Now a slave to my creator —

To his hand I yield up my soul :

His it is for ever to use

For what end he may see fit ;

No more will I hear thy voice,

My God ! my God ! thou art gone hence .

Yet now I can not mourn nor weep —

(20-40 words)

It is interesting to note that there are numerous references to birds and beasts in this psalm, which has led some commentators to suggest that the psalmist was inspired by his contemplation of nature; others think that he was reflecting on the history of Israel as a nation, whose experiences with both friend and foe were akin to those of God’s “birds.” Whatever its source, it is an excellent example of Hebrew parallelism, where each line of verse contains two parts linked by means of a balance or repetition:

I will lift up my eyes to the hills—

 Above the tempest's sweep; and rooted fast,

 Were all the universe. But human clay!
